# Quality Assurance

`customer_support.support_management.quality_assurance` · v1.0.0 · **draft**

**Was this interaction handled the way we would want it handled, regardless of how it ended?**


> Judging how an interaction was conducted, deliberately separated from how it turned out. QA reads a sample of real conversations against a written standard and produces two things: a specific, evidence-anchored account of what happened in each one, and an aggregate read on whether the standard is being met across the queue. It is a teaching instrument that emits a number as a by-product, not a measurement instrument that emits teaching as a by-product — and every characteristic failure of the discipline comes from running it the other way round.

## Expertise applied


## Outcomes

- A sample drawn at random from a defined eligible population, with the drawing rule written down and auditable — not chosen by whoever was already under suspicion.
- Each reviewed interaction scored against a published rubric, with the specific moment in the transcript that produced each mark quoted alongside it.
- A score the agent could have predicted before seeing it. Where they could not, the finding is against the rubric or the calibration, not the agent.
- Reviewer disagreement measured rather than assumed away, so a mark means the same thing whoever gave it.
- Findings routed somewhere that changes behaviour — a coaching conversation, a knowledge edit, a macro rewrite, a process change. A score that goes nowhere is pure cost.
- An explicit standing read on whether the rubric still describes good work for the product as it is now, not as it was when the rubric was written.
- Agents who will still show you their worst ticket. This is the outcome that makes the others possible and the only one that cannot be rebuilt once lost.


## Failure modes

- QA output used as evidence in a performance case. This is THE characteristic failure. The instrument was built for coaching, and the moment it carries consequence, agents stop surfacing their own hard tickets, stop asking for help on the record, and start optimising the rubric instead of the customer. Honest self-reporting ends overnight and does not come back because you promise it will not happen again.
- Sampling that is not random. Reviewing the complained-about, the reopened, or the agents already being watched measures whoever is being watched. It confirms the prior that selected the sample and says nothing about the queue.
- Scoring the outcome instead of the interaction. Agents do not choose their tickets. Someone working a queue of billing disputes and unfixable defects will look worse than someone working password resets while handling the work better, and the score will be attributed to them.
- A rubric agents cannot predict their own score against. If an agent reads back their own reply and cannot guess the mark, the rubric has taught nothing and the score is weather.
- Reviewers who have never calibrated. Two reviewers scoring the same ticket differently is the normal state of any rubric; two reviewers who have never discovered that they do are running a scoring system with no shared meaning, and reporting reviewer variance as agent variance.
- Checkbox dimensions that reward form over judgement — greeting present, name used, article linked — because they are cheap to score. Agents comply, the replies get worse, and the score goes up.
- A rubric long enough that it is never fully applied. Whoever is behind silently truncates it, so the last dimensions get scored from memory and the programme quietly becomes a different rubric per reviewer.
- Reviewing only closed tickets. The worst-handled work is disproportionately the work still open, so closed-only sampling systematically excludes the failures it exists to find.
- Review volume set by reviewer capacity and then reported as if it had been designed. The sample size is whatever the team had time for; the confidence claimed is whatever sounds credible.
- Feedback that reaches the agent long after the interaction, when they cannot remember the ticket. That is archaeology, not coaching, and it converts the whole programme into record-keeping.
- No appeal path. A score that cannot be challenged turns disagreement into contempt for the programme, and loses the single richest source of rubric corrections there is.
- Auto-fail applied to recoverable things — a tone lapse, a missing sign-off. It converts a graded judgement into a coin flip and destroys the rubric's resolution.
- Everyone passing. A distribution piled at the top means either the bar sits below the floor of current practice or reviewers are avoiding the conflict of a low mark. Both cost the same and produce no information.
- The rubric quietly becoming a description of internal preference — our template, our escalation etiquette, our tone — rather than of a good experience, which shows up as a persistent gap against what customers actually say.


## KPIs

| KPI | Unit | Direction | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| review_coverage | percent | target_band | Share of the eligible population reviewed. Only meaningful when reported next to the drawing rule, because coverage without randomness is not coverage. |
| inter_reviewer_agreement | percent | higher_is_better | Agreement between reviewers independently scoring the same interaction. This is the programme's own accuracy; without it every other figure here is unattributable. |
| agent_self_score_gap | index | lower_is_better | Distance between an agent's prediction of their own score and the reviewer's mark. Measures whether the standard transferred, and indicts the rubric before the agent. |
| score_distribution_spread | index | target_band | Whether the rubric discriminates at all. A distribution piled against the ceiling means it is measuring attendance. |
| interaction_to_feedback_latency | days | lower_is_better | Time from the interaction to the agent hearing about it. Feedback decays with distance; late reviews are record-keeping wearing a coaching label. |
| dispute_rate | percent | target_band | Share of scores challenged. Near zero usually means there is no appeal path rather than no disagreement. |
| dispute_upheld_rate | percent | target_band | Share of challenges that changed the score. Calibrates the reviewers, not the agents. |
| coaching_conversion_rate | percent | higher_is_better | Share of reviews that produced a named coaching action, knowledge edit, macro change or process fix. A score that goes nowhere is cost without product. |
| rubric_age | days | lower_is_better | Time since the rubric was last argued against tickets that actually arrived. Rubrics rot silently as the product changes. |
| quality_to_satisfaction_divergence | index | target_band | Standing gap between rubric score and what customers report about the same interactions. A widening gap is a rubric finding first and an agent finding second. |
| open_ticket_share_of_sample | percent | target_band | Share of the reviewed sample that was still open at review time. A figure near nothing means the programme is structurally blind to its worst cases. |

## Metadata

owner **Customer Support** · updated 2026-08-08 · review **unreviewed** · confidence **provisional**


> No thresholds, no sample sizes, no pass marks anywhere in this file — deliberately. How many interactions to review, what counts as agreement, where the bar sits: all of that is Layer 4's arithmetic and belongs in the pack manifest, because all of it is different for a swarming team and an outsourced one. This file declares what the discipline is for and how it fails.
Two authoring decisions worth challenging on review. First, performance_management sits under `parallel` rather than `downstream`, which is a claim about how the world ought to work as much as how it does — plenty of real organisations do feed QA into performance cases, and this file says that when they do, they have stopped running QA. Second, `outsourced_bpo` is listed under applies_to even though QA there is frequently contractual rather than developmental; the heuristics still hold, but the consequence-free assumption behind them often does not, and a BPO branch under models/ should say so.
Nothing here is executable against today's substrate — there is no ticket, conversation, scorecard or satisfaction signal in the pipeline. That constraint lives in the objects and situations, not here; a capability file makes no runtime claims.
